title: The First Forgetting
author: Sandra Boyle
synopsis:
Subtitle: A young woman experiences her first unexplained memory loss — a single missing moment tied to someone she once trusted. At first, she blames stress, distraction, anything rational. But when the forgetting grows, taking pieces of her past she can’t afford to lose, she realizes something deeper is happening.
As autumn settles in, she begins to sense a pattern: the forgetting isn’t random. It’s emotional. And it’s only the beginning.
The First Forgetting is a haunting, atmospheric prequel novella that reveals the origin of the phenomenon

chapters.title: CHAPTER ONE: A Morning Out of Place
chapters.content:
CHAPTER ONE: A Morning Out of Place

Elin Ellingson woke with the distinct sense that something had been moved.

Not in the room.

The room was exactly as she’d left it the night before: journal on the nightstand, curtains half drawn against the early autumn light, a folded sweater draped over the back of the chair where she always left it when she was too tired to put it away properly. The air was still. Familiar. Safe.

Nothing was out of place.

But she was.

She lay there for a long moment, staring at the pale line of sunlight cutting across the ceiling, listening to the quiet hum of the building settling into morning. Pipes clicked somewhere in the walls. A door closed softly down the hall. Someone’s footsteps passed, then faded. Ordinary sounds. Reassuring sounds. The kind that usually confirmed the world had progressed exactly as expected while she slept.

Elin had always trusted mornings. They were dependable. Structured. You woke up as yourself, carrying yesterday intact, even if you didn’t like everything you were carrying.

She waited for that feeling to arrive.

It didn’t.

Instead, there was a gap.

At first it was only a sense of absence she could feel but not name. A hollow space where a memory should have been. She noticed it the way someone notices a missing tooth with their tongue: not painful, not dramatic, just undeniably wrong. A shape without substance. An outline without content.

Her heart beat faster than it should have. She stayed still, as if moving might disturb whatever fragile balance was holding the morning together.

Okay, she told herself. Okay.

People forgot things all the time. Conversations. Details. The exact wording of a sentence. She was busy. She worked long hours. Forgetfulness was human.

She rolled onto her side and scanned the room as if the missing thing might be visible if she looked closely enough. Her gaze passed over familiar objects: the framed photo on the dresser, the lamp she meant to replace, the small stack of unread mail she’d promised herself she’d sort through this weekend.

Everything looked right.

The problem wasn’t the room.

It was her.

She sat up slowly and pressed the heels of her palms into her eyes. When she lowered her hands again, the room snapped back into focus, but the hollow space remained.

Elin exhaled and reached for her phone.

A message from Calla.

Did you talk to him?

The reaction came before the thought.

Her stomach tightened sharply, a reflexive pull low and fast. Her shoulders stiffened. Her breath caught halfway in.

Talk to who?

She didn’t answer right away. She scrolled through the message thread, her thumb moving faster as unease crept in. No earlier texts. No missed calls. No half-finished exchange. Just that single line, sitting there as if it belonged.

She typed back carefully.

Who?

The reply came almost immediately.

Elin. Don’t do this. You said you would.

Cold spread through her chest, thin and precise. Not panic. Something quieter.

She didn’t remember saying anything.

Didn’t remember a conversation. Didn’t remember a promise. Nothing that would lead Calla to sound this frustrated, expectant.

You said you would.

Said what?

Elin stared at the screen until the words blurred. The hollow space inside her mind widened slightly, like a door opening into a room she didn’t want to enter.

She set the phone down and stood.

Her body felt steady, which unsettled her more than dizziness would have. She crossed the room, checked the window latch. Locked. Closet door. Closed. Bathroom light. Off.

She splashed cold water on her face and studied her reflection. Early thirties. Sleep-softened features. A faint crease between her brows she didn’t remember earning.

You’re fine, she told herself.

The reassurance didn’t hold.

Back in the bedroom, she reached for her journal.

It was where she always went when things felt off; when thoughts tangled or emotions refused to line up. Writing didn’t fix anything, but it gave shape to the mess.

She flipped to the last entry.

Two nights ago.

A list of ordinary things. Notes about work. A reminder to call her mother. Nothing that hinted at a confrontation or a promise worth forgetting.

She turned the page.

A single line waited there, written in her own hand.

Don’t forget what he said.

Her breath caught hard enough that she had to grip the edge of the bed.

The handwriting was unmistakably hers. Pressed too hard. Written fast. Urgent.

Who is he?

What did he say?

She didn’t remember writing it. Not the act. Not the feeling that would have driven her to leave herself a warning without context.

Her phone buzzed again, but she didn’t look at it.

This wasn’t stress.

This wasn’t normal forgetfulness.

Something had happened the night before. Something important enough that she’d tried to preserve it and failed.

She closed the journal carefully. The room felt subtly altered now, like a familiar place seen at the wrong time of day.

Outside the window, a single leaf drifted past, yellowed at the edges. The first one she’d noticed this season.

Autumn.

Elin sat on the edge of the bed, journal in one hand, phone in the other, and breathed through the quiet, creeping fear.

If you’re reading this, she thought, echoing the warning without knowing why, it already happened.

She picked up the pen.

I’m writing this because I don’t trust my memory today.

It’s only a moment. A conversation I should remember, but it’s gone.

Not blurred. Not fuzzy.

Just missing.

She paused, then added one more line.

If I forget again, I want proof that this happened.

chapters.title: CHAPTER TWO: The Contradiction
chapters.content:
CHAPTER TWO: The Contradiction

Elin dressed slowly, as if moving too quickly might dislodge something fragile inside her.

The hollow space was still there. Not painful. Not loud. Just present, like a bruise she hadn’t noticed until someone pressed on it. She could feel it when she reached for familiar thoughts, when she tried to replay the simple sequence of the night before. Each attempt ended the same way: smooth blankness, clean and impossible.

She pulled on jeans, a sweater, socks. Muscle memory carried her through the routine while her mind stayed carefully still, afraid that if she pushed too hard, the absence would widen. She moved through her apartment as if it belonged to someone else. Everything familiar, everything correct, and yet slightly misaligned, as if she’d woken into a version of her life that had been copied and set down a fraction of an inch off.

She paused at the mirror in the hallway, brushing her hair with slow strokes. Her eyes looked normal. Her mouth looked normal. The woman staring back at her looked like she could get through a day and answer emails and smile at the right moments.

The only thing wrong was inside her head.

She reached for her phone again, as if the screen might offer an explanation if she stared long enough.

It buzzed immediately, as though Calla had been waiting for her to wake.

Calla: You promised you’d talk to him last night. Don’t pretend you didn’t.

Elin sat on the edge of the bed, the phone suddenly heavy in her hand. The wording stung, not accusatory, exactly, but edged with irritation. With expectation. Calla wasn’t asking if something was wrong. She was responding to a failure. To a choice Elin had apparently made.

Elin typed, erased, typed again.

Elin: I don’t remember that.

She watched the typing bubble appear, disappear, then reappear. Calla was thinking. Or pacing. Or deciding how much patience she had left.

Calla: Elin, you literally said, “I’ll handle it.” You said it twice.

Elin closed her eyes.

She could almost hear herself saying it, the cadence, the calmness, the careful tone she used when she wanted something to stop escalating. She could imagine the situation that would prompt it: Calla upset, Elin stepping in, promising resolution. That was how their dynamic worked. Calla felt the weather; Elin built the shelter.

But the memory itself wasn’t there.

It was like trying to recall a dream someone else had described to her. Familiar, plausible, and completely unreachable.

She pressed her fingers against her temple, hard enough to hurt a little, as if pain might force something loose.

Nothing.

She opened her eyes and stared at the phone again. The words on the screen didn’t change. They didn’t soften. They didn’t offer a clue.

You promised you’d talk to him.

Don’t forget what he said.

The phrases didn’t match. A promise implied a plan. The warning implied a rupture. Both implied a man who mattered enough to destabilize her.

She didn’t have a man like that in her life.

Not anymore.

She stood, forcing herself to move. Standing still made the thoughts circle too tightly, tightening into panic. Motion was control. So she performed the small morning routines, as if repeating them could recreate normalcy.

Downstairs, the kitchen greeted her with ordinary quiet. Morning light spilled across the counter, illuminating dust motes and the faint ring left by a mug she must have used earlier. The smell of last night’s tea lingered faintly, herbal and cooling.

Normal.

Except for the scrap of paper near the sink.

She stopped short.

It was small. Torn from the corner of a notebook page. The edges uneven. She didn’t remember leaving it there, but she already knew what she would find before she picked it up.

Her handwriting.

Don’t forget what he said.

The same words.

Not similar. Not close. Exact.

The note sat in her palm like a dare.

Her stomach tightened, deeper this time, less startled and more unsettled. Two warnings. Same phrasing. Different locations. That wasn’t coincidence. That was intention. It meant she had expected to forget badly enough to leave herself redundant reminders.

She turned the note over.

Blank.

No name. No date. No context.

Nothing that would help.

Elin set the note down carefully, aligning it with the edge of the counter as if order might produce clarity. She pressed her fingertips to the cool surface and breathed slowly, grounding herself in sensation. Cold stone. Solid floor. The steady tick of the kitchen clock.

Think.

She tried to reconstruct the night before again, more methodically this time, as if memory were a file cabinet she could access if she found the right drawer.

She remembered coming home from work. She remembered dropping her bag by the door. She remembered how her shoulders had ached with the tiredness that sank into bone. She remembered boiling water, the kettle’s whistle sharp in the quiet apartment. She remembered standing by the window while the tea steeped, watching the streetlights flicker on.

She remembered sitting on her bed with the journal open, pen resting against the page.

After that?

Nothing.

No blur. No fuzzy edges. Just a clean break, like a film cut mid-scene.

The absence didn’t feel as if she had forgotten. It felt as if an edit had removed something.

Elin’s throat tightened. She took a sip of water she didn’t remember pouring, then set the glass down with more force than necessary.

This wasn’t how tiredness worked.

This wasn’t how distraction worked.

Her phone buzzed again.

Calla: Are you okay?

The shift in tone was subtle but unmistakable. The irritation had given way to concern, which somehow made Elin feel worse. Concern meant Calla was noticing something was off, which meant Elin’s ability to contain this, whatever this was, was already failing.

Elin swallowed and typed back.

Elin: I’m fine. Just tired.

The lie tasted thin. But it was small. Protective. A way to buy time.

She stared at the screen for a moment after sending it, waiting for another message, another push. None came. That silence felt heavy with implication. Calla was choosing to let it go or choosing to watch.

Elin moved through the rest of the morning on instinct. She packed her bag. Checked that the stove was off twice. Paused at the door as if she’d forgotten something and couldn’t name it. Then she forced herself outside.

The air was crisp, carrying the faint scent of wood smoke and damp leaves. Autumn had settled in quietly while she wasn’t paying attention. The trees along the street were still mostly green, but flecks of yellow and rust had appeared, scattered like early warnings.

As she walked, she caught herself cataloging details she would normally ignore. The crunch of leaves underfoot. The pressure of her bag strap on her shoulder. The faint ache in her left knee when she stepped off the curb.

Stay present, she told herself. Stay here.

But her mind kept circling back to the same questions.

Who was he?

And what had he said that warranted a warning she couldn’t remember writing?

She replayed her recent interactions, scanning for likely candidates. A coworker? A former partner? Someone from her past she hoped she was done with? Each possibility slid into the hollow space and vanished, leaving no emotional residue behind.

That frightened her more than the forgetting itself.

She knew her emotional patterns. She always had. She was careful with trust, slow to confront, prone to smoothing things over instead of sharpening them into conflict. If someone had said something important: something threatening, or revelatory, or deeply disappointing, she should feel something about it.

Anger. Sadness. Relief. Disgust.

Instead, there was nothing.

The lack of feeling was its own kind of evidence.

At work, the day unfolded with unsettling normalcy. Emails were answered. Meetings attended. Conversations held. Elin’s hands moved across her keyboard with practiced competence. She smiled at coworkers in the hallway. She answered questions. She nodded at the right places in a meeting, her body performing the motions of a normal day while her mind stayed braced for impact.

The strange part was that no one seemed to notice.

Or maybe they did, and they were polite enough to say nothing.

Calla watched her more closely than usual, Elin realized. Not with obvious scrutiny, but with that quiet attention Calla had always had when she was worried. Elin could feel it across the room like heat.

At one point, Calla appeared beside her desk and leaned in, voice low.

“Are you sure you’re okay?”

Elin looked up and forced her expression into something neutral. “Just didn’t sleep well.”

Another lie. Slightly bigger this time. It carried the implication that it was temporary, that it would pass, that Calla didn’t need to look too closely.

Calla’s gaze held hers for a beat too long. Then she nodded, but the nod looked like agreement she didn’t believe.

“Okay,” Calla said. “If you say so.”

After she walked away, Elin stared at her screen for several seconds without seeing it.

She was already doing what she always did: keeping things contained so no one else had to carry them.

Except now containment felt less like strength and more like refusal.

By midafternoon, the hollow space had stopped feeling contained. It pressed outward, affecting the way she listened, the way she spoke, the way she tracked time. She found herself double-checking things she normally trusted: calendar entries, sent messages, notes she’d scribbled in the margins of documents.

Proof, she realized.

She was already searching for proof.

She checked her sent emails from the previous night, half expecting to find something she didn’t remember writing. There was nothing unusual. She checked her calendar. Nothing out of the ordinary. She checked her call log. Nothing.

The absence of evidence should have reassured her.

Instead, it made her feel more alone.

That evening, back in her apartment, she spread the journal, the scrap of paper, and her phone on the table like evidence in a case she wasn’t qualified to investigate. Three objects. All contradicting her internal experience.

Her handwriting didn’t lie.

Calla didn’t lie.

Which left only one conclusion she wasn’t ready to accept.

That her mind had failed her.

Elin stared at the journal again, tracing the ink with her eyes.

Don’t forget what he said.

The words felt heavier now, weighted with implication. She had known she would forget. She had expected it. Which meant this wasn’t an accident.

It was a pattern, or the beginning of one.

She sat still and tried to imagine herself writing that line last night. What would it have taken? What kind of conversation would make her warn her future self?

She pictured sitting on the edge of the bed with the pen in her hand, breath shallow, heart racing. She pictured the impulse to write something down before it slipped away. She pictured a voice: male, close; familiar enough to matter, saying something that landed too sharply to absorb.

She couldn’t hear the words. But she could feel the shape of the reaction she might have had.

Not anger.

Not fear.

Something quieter.

Disappointment, maybe. The kind that rearranged your understanding of someone without permission.

Elin closed the journal and pressed her palms flat against the table, grounding herself in the moment's solidity.

Whatever this was, it wasn’t over.

And the worst part wasn’t the missing memory.

It was the growing certainty that it wouldn’t be the last one.

She looked down at the scrap of paper again. The redundancy of the warning felt almost tender, like a version of herself trying to protect her from something she had no words for.

Elin picked up the note and held it between her fingers, watching it tremble slightly with her breath.

“I don’t know what you’re doing,” she whispered, not sure if she meant herself or the thing inside her that had removed the memory, “but I know you did it.”

Outside, the wind moved through the trees, shaking loose another leaf. It drifted past the window, slow and unhurried, like the first one had.

Autumn was settling in.

And now Elin understood something she hadn’t been able to admit that morning.

This wasn’t a single lapse.

Elin closed the journal and did not put it away.

chapters.title: CHAPTER THREE: Containment
chapters.content:
CHAPTER THREE: Containment

Elin decided to test herself.

The decision arrived without panic or ceremony. It didn’t feel brave. It felt procedural. If something in her mind was misfiring, then the sensible response was observation. Measurement. Control.

That was how she handled problems. She gathered information and adjusted.

The forgetting, she told herself, deserved the same treatment.

She waited until morning.

The night passed without incident: no remembered dreams, no sudden returns of clarity. When she woke, the hollow space was still there, unchanged. It hadn’t grown. It hadn’t receded. It simply existed, like a structural flaw she’d only just noticed.

She sat up in bed and resisted the urge to reach for her phone.

Instead, she chose a marker.

Something ordinary. Something neutral. Something that should be easy to verify later.

She picked the mug.

Blue. Ceramic. Chipped at the rim. The one she reached for most mornings because it fit her hand and held heat longer than the others.

She filled it with coffee slowly, narrating the steps under her breath as she went. The smell. The warmth through the handle. The faint ring of moisture where she set it down.

“Blue mug. Coffee. Morning,” she said quietly.

Then she took a photo of it.

The act felt ridiculous. Reassuring.

She left the apartment.

On the walk to work, she created more markers. The cracked sidewalk at the corner. The café with mismatched chairs. The tree was already turning while the rest of the block stayed green. She checked the time at each point and wrote it into her notes app without opening it to read back.

At work, she escalated the test.

She scheduled an email to herself for noon. One sentence. Nothing emotional.

Blue mug this morning.

She attended meetings. Answered messages. Took notes she didn’t need. Before lunch, she wrote a brief reminder on a sticky note and placed it beneath her keyboard, face down.

At noon, she paused.

She closed her eyes. Counted three breaths.

Blue mug.Coffee.Morning.

The memory returned intact.

Her phone chimed.

The scheduled email arrived exactly when it should have.

Relief settled in; not sharp, not euphoric. Controlled.

See? she thought. This is manageable.

The thought stayed with her longer than it should have.

That afternoon, she raised the difficulty.

She initiated a conversation with a coworker about a timeline change, nothing emotional but involving decision and agreement. Before leaving the conversation, she sent herself another delayed message with a single phrase from it.

Later, in the bathroom, she replayed the exchange. The words came back. The tone. The conclusion.

Her phone chimed again.

Match confirmed.

Again, relief.

And beneath it, something else.

Unease.

The tests were working too well.

Which meant the forgetting wasn’t random.

Which meant it was choosing.

She told herself she was overthinking it.

That evening, Calla texted.

Do you want to come by tonight?

Elin stopped moving.

This was a different kind of test.

She could tell Calla. Frame it lightly. Let it exist outside her own head.

She typed.

Maybe. Long day.

Didn’t send it.

Another message arrived.

You’ve been quiet.

Quiet was Calla’s word for distance. For something being wrong.

Elin set the phone down on the counter and leaned back against it, closing her eyes.

If she told Calla, the problem would leave the realm of observation.

If she didn’t, she could keep testing. Keep control.

She picked up the phone again.

I’m okay. Just tired. Rain check?

She sent it before she could reconsider.

The reply came a minute later.

Okay. Let me know.

No pressure. No interrogation. Just trust.

The trust sat heavily in Elin’s chest.

She made dinner. Ate mechanically. Cleaned the kitchen with deliberate care. She moved through the apartment the way she always did; efficient, contained, intact.

Later, she opened her journal.

She didn’t write about the tests in detail. She didn’t catalog results. That felt too permanent.

Instead, she wrote:

I tested myself today. It worked.

She stared at the sentence.

Then added:

That should make me feel better.

She closed the journal without writing what followed.

She aligned it carefully on the nightstand, squared to the edge. Control, in small ways, still felt possible.

As she turned off the light, a realization caught her breath.

She wasn’t afraid of forgetting.

She was afraid of how easily she was learning to live around it.

Containment, she understood now, was not safety.

But it was close enough that she was willing to pretend.

chapters.title: CHAPTER FOUR: The Denial Phase
chapters.content:
CHAPTER FOUR: The Denial Phase

Elin decided not to panic.

It was a conscious choice; made with the same restraint she used to ignore a strange noise in the house or an unfamiliar ache that might disappear if left alone. Panic would only invite questions she wasn’t prepared to answer, questions that demanded clarity she didn’t yet trust.

There were explanations for memory gaps. Stress. Fatigue. Emotional overload. She had read enough, absorbed enough secondhand expertise to know the mind protected itself in strange ways. Forgetting wasn’t always failure. Sometimes it was a form of triage.

She repeated that to herself in the shower, letting hot water loosen the tension in her shoulders. Steam fogged the mirror, blurring her reflection until she looked like a suggestion rather than a person. She wiped a clear patch with her hand and met her own eyes.

See? she told herself. You’re fine.

She dressed carefully, soft sweater, worn jeans, familiar boots. Nothing new. Nothing sharp. She wanted no friction against her skin, no reminder that things could feel wrong without explanation.

In the kitchen, she restored order where she could. Dishes washed. Counter wiped. The journal placed neatly on the nightstand instead of left open like an accusation. She folded the loose scrap of paper and tucked it inside, telling herself it made sense to keep the warnings together.

Containment felt reasonable.Responsible.

Before leaving, she hesitated, phone in hand. For a moment, she considered setting another reminder. Another test. Something she could check later.

She didn’t.

That, too, was a decision.

By the time she arrived at work, she had nearly convinced herself the morning had been an anomaly. An off day. If she didn’t give it weight, it would lose its power.

Calla was already at her desk, coffee in hand, posture alert in a way Elin recognized instantly.

“You good?” Calla asked, casual but not careless.

“I’m just tired,” Elin said, without breaking stride.

Calla studied her a beat too long. “You’ve been saying that a lot.”

Elin smiled, light and practiced. “Occupational hazard.”

It wasn’t entirely untrue. Truth-adjacent statements were easier to carry.

The morning unfolded in routines Elin leaned into deliberately: emails answered, meetings attended, tasks completed. Structure carried her forward without asking questions. As long as she stayed in motion, the hollow space remained contained.

Denial, she told herself, wasn’t refusal.It was delay.

Around midday, Calla appeared at her desk again.

“You want to grab lunch?” Calla asked. “Just us.”

Elin hesitated, only a second, but it was enough.

“Sure,” she said quickly.

They walked to the café they’d been going to for years. Familiar tables. Familiar menu. Elin ordered without looking, grateful for the ease of saying the words.

They sat by the window. Leaves skittered across the sidewalk outside, dry and restless.

Calla stirred her soup once, then again.

“So,” she said. “Did you talk to him?”

The question landed softly, but it didn’t bounce.

“No,” Elin said. “I didn’t.”

“You said you would.”

“I know. I just… didn’t get to it.”

“That’s not like you.”

Elin smiled faintly. “People change.”

Calla didn’t return the smile.

“You were upset,” Calla said. “You asked me what you should do.”

Elin felt her pulse quicken. “Upset how?”

Calla paused, choosing carefully. “Quiet upset. Which is usually worse.”

Elin took a sip of water, steadying the glass with both hands.

“I don’t remember that conversation,” she said.

Calla’s posture shifted, alert now. “None of it?”

“No.”

“You said he crossed a line,” Calla continued. “You didn’t give details. Just that you couldn’t ignore it.”

Elin’s chest tightened. “And what did you tell me?”

“That you already knew what you needed to do.”

That felt true in a way Elin couldn’t explain, and that frightened her more than contradiction.

“I’m sure it was a misunderstanding,” Elin said carefully. “Something that felt bigger in the moment.”

Calla watched her. “You don’t usually talk yourself out of things that fast.”

Elin shrugged. “Maybe I should.”

Calla didn’t argue.

Which felt like a failure, even as Elin told herself it was relief.

Back at work, Elin doubled down on competence. She reviewed documents, summarized meetings in follow-up emails, documented decisions that had just been made. Evidence, again. Professionalism masquerading as control.

When she caught herself noting trivial details, the exact time she left a meeting, who had spoken first, she stopped and closed the notebook.

Enough, she told herself.

At home that evening, she opened the journal.

She reread the earlier warning, then wrote beneath it, her handwriting measured and calm.

You’re tired. You’re overwhelmed. Memory gaps happen. Don’t overreact.

The words looked sensible. Comforting. The kind of advice she’d give anyone else.

She closed the journal, satisfied.

Later, lying in bed, sleep wouldn’t come. Her thoughts circled carefully, avoiding the hollow space. She focused instead on Calla’s words.

He crossed a line.

What line?

Elin prided herself on adaptability. On giving people grace. If she’d labeled something a line, it meant it had mattered.

She turned onto her side, pressing her hand to her chest.

If this was denial, she reasoned, it was temporary. Strategic.

She would face the truth when it demanded her.

Just not yet.

Outside, wind moved through the trees, leaves scraping along the pavement. Autumn settling in.

Elin closed her eyes and chose sleep over questions.

Chose forgetting over disruption.

For now.

chapters.title: CHAPTER FIVE: The First Journal Entry
chapters.content:
CHAPTER FIVE: The First Journal Entry

Elin did not open the journal right away.

She left it where it was on the nightstand and moved through the apartment instead, turning lights on and off, touching familiar surfaces as if they might reassure her through repetition. The couch armrest. The edge of the kitchen counter. The cool metal of the refrigerator handle.

Everything responded the way it always had.

It was her trust in those responses that felt newly compromised.

She made tea she didn’t want and carried it into the living room, setting the mug down without drinking it. The apartment was quiet in the way it always was at night, not empty, but settled. The kind of quiet she usually appreciated. The kind that made space for thought.

Tonight, it pressed in on her.

Elin sat on the couch and tried, one last time, to reconstruct the missing memory.

She did not force it. She had learned that pushing only tightened the blankness, like gripping sand too hard. Instead, she let her mind move loosely, circling the edges of the absence, hoping something might surface on its own.

She pictured the night before in fragments. Coming home. The weight of her bag sliding off her shoulder. The kettle whistling. The way the light in the bedroom looked slightly dimmer than usual, as if the day had already begun to fold in on itself.

She could picture herself sitting on the bed.

She could picture the journal open.

She could not picture why.

Her throat tightened.

The problem was no longer that she couldn’t remember.

The problem was that she couldn’t tell whether she ever would.

Elin leaned forward and rested her elbows on her knees, pressing her palms together until the pressure grounded her. This wasn’t panic, she told herself. Panic would be louder. More urgent. This was something else.

Assessment.

She had always been good at assessment. Breaking problems down into manageable parts. Identifying variables. Deciding what could be controlled and what could not.

Right now, there was only one thing she knew for certain:

Her memory could not be trusted.

The thought settled heavily, not with fear, but with finality.

She stood and crossed the room, stopping in front of the nightstand. The journal waited there, its leather cover catching the lamplight softly. She had owned it for years. It had always been a place for reflection, not evidence.

Tonight, it felt different.

She picked it up and turned it over in her hands, noting the worn edges, the way the spine bent easily where it had been opened a thousand times before. This journal knew her habits. Her moods. Her voice.

That was the problem.

If she were going to write something down now, it couldn’t be the kind of writing she did when she was processing feelings. It had to be something else.

A record.

She opened to a blank page and stared at it.

The urge to soften what she wrote was immediate and familiar. To contextualize. To explain. To reassure herself with language that suggested this was temporary, manageable, nothing to worry about.

She resisted it.

Instead, she asked herself a simpler question.

What do I know?

The answer was uncomfortable in its brevity.

Very little.

Elin lifted the pen and hovered over the page, waiting for the right words. None came. Her thoughts felt slippery, refusing to line up into anything coherent. She could feel the old instinct rising; the desire to close the journal, to tell herself she was overreacting, to leave this for tomorrow when it would look smaller.

Tomorrow was no longer a guarantee.

She wrote anyway.

I’m writing this down because I don’t trust my memory today.

The sentence looked stark on the page, stripped of qualifiers. She paused, her pen hovering, surprised by the quiet weight of what she’d just admitted.

It’s only a moment, a conversation I should remember, but it’s gone.

She stopped again.

Seeing the words outside her head changed something. The absence became real in a way it hadn’t been when it lived only inside her. Documented, it could no longer be explained away as mood or imagination.

Not blurred. Not fuzzy. Just… missing.

Her hand tightened around the pen.

I keep waiting for it to come back. That feels reasonable. Like something that should happen if I stay calm.

The familiar logic steadied her. Calm had always been her ally. Calm kept things contained.

If I forget again, I want proof that this happened.

The pen slowed.

That I didn’t imagine the gap.

She sat back, reading the entry through once, then again. It wasn’t dramatic. It wasn’t panicked. It was careful and restrained, which made it more frightening than anything she could have written in a rush of emotion.

This wasn’t how people wrote when they were anxious.

This was how people wrote when they were preparing.

Elin closed the journal and rested her hand on the cover, feeling the faint warmth left by the lamp. A subtle tremor moved through her fingers, too small to be called shaking.

She stood and paced the length of the apartment; the journal tucked under her arm like something she needed to keep close. She thought of Calla, the way her sister looked at her that afternoon, watchful and unconvinced.

She could tell her now.

She could send a message. Something vague, but honest. Something that would invite concern without explanation.

She pictured Calla’s response immediately. The questions. The worry. The insistence that Elin see someone, talk to someone, do something.

Elin stopped pacing.

The journal felt heavier in her hands.

If she told Calla, this would stop being hers to manage.

And she wasn’t ready for that.

She returned the journal to the nightstand, placing it carefully where she could see it from the bed. Not hidden. Not open. Available.

A compromise.

She changed into pajamas and climbed into bed, leaving the light on longer than usual. The quiet pressed in again, but this time it felt different, less empty, more watchful.

She reached for her phone, half expecting another message. There was nothing.

Good, she thought, and immediately hated herself for the relief.

Elin turned onto her side and stared at the wall, the journal within her peripheral vision. The first journal entry sat there now, static and undeniable. A marker placed deliberately in time.

She had crossed a line she couldn’t uncross.

From this point forward, she would not be able to say she hadn’t known something was wrong.

The thought should have scared her more than it did.

Instead, it brought a strange sense of clarity.

If her memory could not be trusted, then she would build something that could.

Outside, the wind rose again, stirring the trees. A leaf scraped along the pavement below her window, the sound sharp in the quiet.

Elin closed her eyes.

This was not panic.

This was preparation.

And she felt she had just taken the first step into something that would follow her for years.

chapters.title: CHAPTER SIX: Conflicting Accounts
chapters.content:
CHAPTER SIX: Conflicting Accounts

Elin stopped trusting silence.

Silence had always been her refuge: the space where thoughts settled, where emotions arranged themselves into something manageable. Now it felt porous. Too much could pass through it without leaving a mark.

She arrived at work early, hoping routine would steady her. The office was quiet, lights dimmed, desks still untouched. Systems hummed softly, cycling through tasks without attention. She liked that. Fewer variables.

She sat at her desk and opened her notebook.

Date. Time.

She wrote them carefully, then paused.

I remember waking up.I remember leaving the apartment.

She stopped there. Writing more felt like tempting something.

By midmorning, the office filled around her. Elin listened more than she spoke, tracking tone and timing with a vigilance she hadn’t needed before.

The first contradiction surfaced in a meeting she’d attended dozens of times.

“So, like we discussed yesterday,” a colleague said, shuffling papers, “we’ll move forward with the revised timeline.”

Elin looked up. “Yesterday?”

Her colleague blinked. “After lunch. You were there.”

“I don’t remember that meeting.”

The room didn’t freeze. It simply adjusted.

Calla spoke from across the table. “You sat right there.”

Elin glanced at the chair. Her stomach tightened.

“You asked questions,” someone added. “Good ones.”

“What kind of questions?” Elin asked.

Calla hesitated, only a beat. “About communication. About impact.”

That sounded like her.

“I don’t remember any of it,” Elin said.

A soft laugh followed. “Long week.”

The meeting moved on.

Elin took notes on decisions that were already made. She felt as though she were being briefed on her own past, always arriving a step late.

Afterward, Calla followed her to her desk.

“You’re really not joking, are you?” Calla asked.

“No.”

“You were engaged,” Calla said carefully. “Focused. You didn’t seem off.”

“That makes it worse,” Elin said.

Calla didn’t argue.

The rest of the day unfolded in fragments. Small references Elin couldn’t place. Tasks she’d apparently completed. Agreements she didn’t remember consenting to.

Each time, she adjusted.

Each time, she let the shared version of events take precedence.

By early afternoon, she was documenting things as they happened. Names. Times. Decisions. Not obsessively. Just enough to keep herself oriented.

She was still functioning.

That was what frightened her.

By the time she got home, her head ached with the effort of maintaining continuity she no longer trusted.

She went straight to the journal.

On a fresh page, she wrote:

Other people remember things I do not.

She paused, then added:

They remember me being present.

That distinction mattered.

She wasn’t disappearing. She was participating, competently, and forgetting anyway.

Her phone buzzed.

I’m coming over, Calla wrote.

Elin didn’t argue.

They ate in near silence. Finally, Calla said, “You should see someone.”

“I will,” Elin said. “If this keeps happening.”

Calla met her gaze. “Elin.”

“I just need to understand what’s happening first.”

“That it’s real?” Calla asked.

“Yes.”

Calla nodded. “It is.”

“And you trust your memory?”

“Yes.”

The certainty in her voice landed hard.

If other people remembered Elin’s life more clearly than she did, then authority over her own experience had already begun to slip.

After Calla left, the apartment felt less anchored.

Elin opened the journal again and wrote:

If my memory and the world disagree, the world will win.

She stared at the sentence.

Then added:

I need proof. Not reassurance.

She slid the journal beneath the bed, farther back than before. Not out of fear.

Out of necessity.

As she turned off the lights, she felt the familiar tug at the edge of her awareness. Something loosening. Something drifting.

She didn’t stop it.

Outside, the wind moved through the trees, carrying away leaves that had held on longer than they should have.

This time, the contradictions were no longer just inside her.

They were shared.

chapters.title: CHAPTER SEVEN: The First Emotional Trigger
chapters.content:
CHAPTER SEVEN: The First Emotional Trigger

Elin felt it before she understood it.

The sensation arrived as a tightening, an inward draw, like a muscle bracing for impact. Her shoulders stiffened. Her breath caught just slightly. It was the same reflex she had learned to trust over years of quiet observation; the one that warned her disappointment was coming before her mind could catch up.

She did not look surprised.

That, later, would bother her most.

They were sitting in a small conference room on the third floor; the kind designed for conversations that weren’t meant to linger. Neutral walls. A table too large for the number of people present. A box of tissues placed deliberately within reach, as if expecting emotion while pretending it would not be required.

He sat across from her.

She noticed absently that his posture was relaxed. Open. One arm draped casually over the back of his chair, legs crossed at the ankle. He did not look like someone preparing to say something that would matter.

That should have been her first warning.

“I just want to be clear,” he said, voice even, reasonable. “This isn’t personal.”

Elin nodded.

She always nodded at that part. Everyone said it the same way, as if saying it first transformed intention into truth. As if neutrality were declared, not earned.

“I think we all agree this is for the best,” he continued. “Given the circumstances.”

“What circumstances?” she asked.

Her voice sounded steady to her own ears. Calm. Interested. She noted the steadiness with mild detachment, the way she might notice her pulse slowing after a climb.

He hesitated.

Just a fraction of a second. Barely enough to register. But Elin had always been good at noticing fractions.

“Well,” he said, smiling faintly, “the ones we discussed.”

The hollow space stirred.

She waited.

For context. For memory. For the shape of the conversation, he was referencing to rise and fill the absence.

Nothing came.

“I’m not sure I follow,” she said carefully.

His smile tightened into mild irritation. The kind that came from believing he was being patient with someone who was not keeping up.

“You were very clear yesterday,” he said.

Something cold slid through her chest.

“Clear about what?” she asked.

He leaned back, folding his hands together, settling into explanation mode. “That you understood my position. That you didn’t want to complicate things.”

The words landed one by one, each finding a place to settle.

“You said you could live with it,” he added, almost kindly. “That you always do.”

There it was.

Not shouted. Not dramatic. Not even cruel in the way people expected cruelty to look.

Just precise enough to cut.

Elin felt the disappointment register fully this time: clean, sharp, unmistakable. It wasn’t about the content of what he was saying. It was about the assumption beneath it.

That she would absorb the cost.

That she would translate harm into understanding.

That her silence was consent rather than restraint.

She had seen this pattern before. In others. In herself. The way expectations calcified around her because she rarely pushed back. Because she listened. Because she made space.

Because she had learned, long ago, that wanting less was safer than wanting more.

“I don’t think that’s what I said,” she replied.

Her voice remained even. That, too, would bother her later.

He frowned slightly, the faintest crease appearing between his brows. “Elin, we talked about this. You said you didn’t want to make it a bigger issue.”

Her heart pounded.

The room seemed to narrow; the walls drawing imperceptibly closer. She searched his face, looking for something she could anchor to: familiarity, care, even defensiveness.

Instead, she saw certainty.

“You didn’t ask me what I wanted,” she drawled.

The words surprised her with their clarity.

He sighed.

The sound was heavy with practiced patience. “You never said you wanted anything different.”

Something in her chest fractured.

Not loudly. Not violently.

Just a soft, internal click. A realization settling into place.

This was the line.

This was what Calla had meant.

He spoke about her reaction as if it had already been decided. As if her discomfort were a misunderstanding they had resolved.

She had trusted him with her restraint, her willingness to consider his position, her tendency to listen first. And he had mistaken that trust for permission.

She felt the forgetting begin almost immediately.

Not as a sudden drop. Not as darkness.

As a fade.

The edges of the conversation softened. The sharpness dulled. The words lost their weight even as they continued to be spoken. She could still hear him. Still respond. Still nod at the right moments.

Her emotional core felt wronged, diminished, unseen. All the feelings slipped away from her awareness like a tide pulling back from the shore.

She tried to hold on to it.

Tried to memorize the feeling. The betrayal. The way his assumption had landed inside her with such quiet violence.

But it was already going.

The disappointment thinned, draining of color and urgency, leaving behind something vague and manageable. A discomfort she could live with. A dullness she recognized.

Too manageable.

By the time the conversation ended, by the time she stood and gathered her things, the clarity had dulled into something she could almost dismiss.

Almost.

She walked back to her desk on autopilot, body moving through familiar paths without instruction. She sat down, opened her notebook, and stared at the blank page.

What just happened?

She reached for the memory and felt her fingers close on air.

Her pulse spiked.

This time, she didn’t rationalize it away.

This time, she knew.

She closed the notebook and reached for her journal instead, hands trembling now, the steadiness of earlier days finally gone. She flipped it open and began writing without pausing.

This just happened.

She pressed harder, the pen biting into the paper.

I was disappointed. Deeply. By him.

She forced herself to keep going, even as the feeling slipped further out of reach.

He assumed I would accept less. He assumed I would carry it.

Her breath came fast, shallow.

Already, the words felt flatter than they should have. Less charged. Less alive.

The forgetting was faster this time.

She wrote one last line; the pen shaking now.

I am writing this before it disappears.

When she leaned back, heart hammering, the room felt unnaturally calm. The emotional storm had passed too quickly, leaving behind a quiet, unsettling clarity.

This wasn’t random.

It wasn’t delayed.

Emotion triggered forgetting.

Not stress. Not fear. Not exhaustion.

Disappointment.

Betrayal.

The kind that threatened to rearrange how she saw someone.

She closed the journal and pressed it to her chest, grounding herself in its weight. The leather was warm from her hands. Solid. Real.

She wasn’t losing her mind.

Her mind was protecting her.

The realization settled heavily.

Because protection implied intent.

And intent meant this wasn’t something she could wish away.

That night, sleep came in fragments. Every time she drifted toward rest, she felt the memory tug again, thinning, retreating further into the hollow space. She stopped fighting it somewhere after midnight, exhaustion winning out over vigilance.

By morning, she knew she could not fully recall what he had said.

Only that it had mattered.

Only that she had been right to write it down.

She woke with the same hollow ache she had felt days before.

This time, she reached for the journal before she reached for reassurance.

Instructions for Myself

Elin did not mark the day.

That omission was deliberate.

Dates made things feel official, fixed in time. She wasn’t ready for that yet. She wanted this moment to exist slightly out of sequence, the way the forgetting already did: unmoored, difficult to pin down, resistant to order.

She sat on the floor of her bedroom with the journal open in her lap, back against the side of the bed, knees drawn up. The room was dim, lit only by the lamp on the nightstand. Outside, the evening wind moved through the trees, lifting leaves that scraped softly along the sidewalk below.

The sound anchored her.

She had quickly learned that anchoring mattered.

The forgetting had taken nothing else today. Not in the obvious sense. She could recall her morning. Her commute. The meeting. The conversation that had fractured something inside her. She could still replay the shape of it, even if the emotional weight had dulled.

But she could feel the erosion.

The edges were already thinning.

She pressed the journal flatter against her thighs and stared at the page. The blankness did not intimidate her the way it used to. It felt… expectant. As if it knew why she was here.

She lifted the pen, then hesitated.

This wasn’t the same as the other entries.

This wasn’t observation.

This was preparation.

She started with something simple.

If you’re reading this, it means I didn’t trust myself to remember.

The words looked stark. Uncomfortable. She sat with them for a moment, letting the admission settle.

She had trusted her mind implicitly for as long as she could remember. Memory had been her proof of continuity; of selfhood, of experience, of cause and effect. To write that sentence was to acknowledge that trust had been broken.

Not shattered.

But compromised.

I’m not writing because I’m panicking. I’m writing because I’m adapting.

She paused, surprised by the steadiness of her own voice on the page. There was no drama in it. No urgency. Just clarity.

That clarity frightened her.

She had always adapted quickly. That had been her strength. She adjusted expectations, absorbed disappointments, recalibrated relationships. She did not demand. She did not insist.

She endured.

And now her mind was doing the same thing.

She wrote again.

The forgetting doesn’t hurt. That’s important.

Her hand slowed.

That might be the most dangerous part.

She stopped and closed her eyes, checking in with herself honestly. The memory of the conversation earlier: the betrayal, the assumption, was still present, but distant. Muted. It no longer burned.

Relief followed almost immediately.

She hadn’t wanted to admit that before.

I felt relief when it faded.

The pen pressed harder against the paper.

That scares me more than the forgetting itself.

She leaned her head back against the bed frame and exhaled slowly. The truth of that sentence resonated deep in her chest. Relief meant the erasure was effective. Efficient. Protective.

And protection could become a preference.

I think my mind is choosing for me when I won’t choose for myself.

That thought lingered.

She had not confronted him fully. She had not insisted on being heard. She had not demanded clarity or accountability. She had done what she always did: absorbed, understood, adjusted.

And her mind had stepped in to finish the job.

She flipped back a few pages, rereading the earlier entries. The first warning. The documentation of absence. The note about other people remembering things she did not.

There was a progression there.

Not chaos.

Logic.

She returned to the current page.

I need you to understand something I might not want to understand later.

She underlined the sentence once, then again.

This is not random.

She wrote slowly now, choosing each word with care.

The forgetting happens when something would force me to change how I see someone.

Not when I’m tired. Not when I’m stressed. Not when I’m overwhelmed.

When I’m disappointed to require action.

She swallowed.

Action had always been the hardest part.

It was easier to let feelings settle quietly than to disrupt the structure of a relationship. Easier to accept less than to risk loss. Easier to reinterpret harm than to name it.

She had learned that early.

I think my mind is protecting me from choices I don’t want to make.

The sentence sat there, heavy and undeniable.

If that was true; if forgetting was not failure but intervention, then she had a distinct problem than she had first believed.

She wasn’t losing control.

She was surrendering it.

She shifted on the floor, legs tingling from disuse, and continued writing.

If you’re reading this and wondering whether it’s still happening, here’s what you should check first.

She paused, then listed.

Are you feeling calm in a situation that should feel wrong? Are you telling yourself it “wasn’t that bad”? Are other people remembering your reactions more clearly than you do?

She stared at the list, recognizing herself in every question.

If yes, assume you forgot something important.

Her hand trembled slightly as she wrote the next line.

Do not assume forgetting means it wasn’t real.

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees, grounding herself in the moment's physicality. The pen. The paper. The pressure.

This was the first time she had written directly to herself rather than about herself.

That distinction mattered.

I know you’ll want proof. You’ll want to be reasonable. You’ll want to explain it away.

She almost smiled at that. The familiarity of her own habits.

Don’t.

She underlined the word once.

Trust the journal more than your instincts.

That line took longer to write.

It went against everything she believed about herself. Her instincts had always been reliable. Quiet, but accurate. Now even those were being filtered.

She continued.

If you’re tempted to stop writing because it feels excessive, that’s a sign you should keep going.

She shifted again; the room growing darker as the evening deepened. The lamplight pooled warmly around her, the rest of the apartment receding into shadow.

She felt strangely calm.

Not numb.

Focused.

This is what preparation feels like, she realized. Not fear. Not urgency. Just resolve.

She wrote one last section, slower than the rest.

I don’t know how long this will last. I don’t know if it will get worse. I don’t know if I’ll forget this entry too.

But I know this:

Silence makes it easier for my mind to erase things. Writing makes it harder.

She sat with that for a long moment, listening to the wind outside, the steady rhythm of leaves loosening and falling.

Autumn had always been her favorite season. The clarity of it. The permission to let go.

She wondered when letting go had felt like disappearance.

She added one last line at the bottom of the page.

If you’re reading this, please don’t ignore it.

She closed the journal carefully, as if sealing something fragile inside. For the first time since the forgetting began, she slid the journal into her bag instead of leaving it at home.

Not hidden.

Accessible.

She stood slowly, joints stiff, and moved through the apartment, turning lights off, leaving the lamp by the bed for last. The room looked unchanged. Ordinary.

But she felt different.

Not broken.

Prepared.

As she climbed into bed, she felt the familiar hollow space stir again, not aggressively, not urgently. Just present.

She did not fight it.

She had learned something important.

The forgetting could take memories.

But it could not take the instructions she left behind.

Not yet.

Outside, the wind rose once more, carrying another scatter of leaves into the street.

Elin closed her eyes.

Whatever happened next, she would not face it entirely alone.

She had left herself a trail.

chapters.title: CHAPTER EIGHT: The Missing Evening
chapters.content:
CHAPTER EIGHT: The Missing Evening

Elin knew the evening was gone before she knew how it had gone.

The awareness arrived without panic, without confusion, just a heavy, settled certainty that someone had removed something wholesale. Not thinned. Not softened. Taken.

She stood in her kitchen, still wearing her coat, keys dangling from her fingers, staring at the digital clock on the stove.

10:47 p.m.

That wasn’t right.

The last thing she remembered was leaving work. Late, but not that late. The sky had been dimming, the air cool against her face. She remembered locking her office door. Remembered the sound of the elevator arriving.

After that—

Nothing.

Her throat tightened.

She set the keys down carefully, as if a sudden movement might fracture something further. Her bag slipped from her shoulder and hit the floor with a dull thud; she felt more than heard it .

“Okay,” she said aloud. The word echoed slightly in the quiet apartment. “Okay.”

She tried to reconstruct the evening the way she’d learned to do now: slowly, methodically, without expectation.

Leaving the building.

Walking to the car.

Driving home.

Dinner.

Time passing.

Each step dissolved as soon as she reached for it.

This wasn’t the clean hollow she’d felt before. This was a cliff's edge.

Her pulse raced, sharp and insistent. She forced herself to breathe, pressing her palm flat against the counter to steady herself.

You’re here now, she told herself. You’re safe.

She checked her phone.

No missed calls. No urgent messages. A few notifications she didn’t remember reading. One text from Calla, time-stamped 8:12 p.m.

You home?

Elin stared at it.

She didn’t remember receiving it. Didn’t remember responding.

She scrolled.

There was a reply.

Yes. Just got in. I’ll call you tomorrow.

She read the line again.

That was her voice. Her phrasing. The message she sent when she wanted to end a conversation gently.

She didn’t remember sending it.

She sank into the nearest chair; phone clutched in both hands. The room felt suddenly too quiet, the air thick and unmoving.

An entire evening.

Gone.

This wasn’t a flicker. This wasn’t emotional residue slipping away.

This was a removal.

Her gaze drifted instinctively toward the bedroom.

The journal.

She moved toward it quickly now, no longer cautious. She dropped to her knees and pulled open the drawer beneath the bed, fingers shaking as she flipped the journal open.

The page she’d last written on was no longer the last entry.

Her breath caught hard in her chest.

There were two pages filled in handwriting she recognized as her own.

The ink was dark. Pressed hard. The words urgent, angled slightly upward as if written in haste.

She scanned them desperately.

I am losing time.

Not fragments. Not moments. Hours.

I noticed it when I checked the clock. It is already late. I do not remember the last several hours.

Her vision blurred. She wiped her eyes with the back of her hand and kept reading.

I believe I confronted him again tonight. I do not know why. I only knew I felt compelled to say something before I forgot.

She swallowed.

I was calmer than I expected to be. That scares me.

The room felt distant now, as if she were reading about someone else.

He said something else. Something worse. Something that confirmed what I already suspected.

Her heart hammered.

I am writing this quickly. The forgetting is faster now.

Elin pressed her hand flat against the page, grounding herself in the physicality of it. This wasn’t speculation. This wasn’t fear.

This was documentation.

I think the forgetting accelerates when I challenge it.

A sharp sound escaped her; half breath, half laugh, entirely unsteady.

Of course.

Of course, the cost of resistance was erasure.

She flipped the page.

If you are reading this, you have lost tonight.

She went still.

I am afraid.

The sentence was simple. Bare. No qualifiers. No rationalization.

I have hidden this journal again.Not from you; from the version of us that will want this to be easier.

If you are calm right now, if this feels excessive or unreasonable, that is exactly why it cannot stay where you can reach it without thinking.

She felt a pain in the middle of her abdomen.

She scanned the room frantically, searching for clues; something out of place, something she didn’t remember doing.

The bed was neatly made. The kitchen clean. Too clean.

She stood, heart pounding, and searched.

Closet. Bathroom cabinet. Behind the books on the shelf.

Nothing.

Panic flared fully now, hot and sharp.

She dropped back onto the bed; her journal clutched against her chest. Her breathing came fast and shallow, the edges of the room shimmering slightly.

This was the point denial failed.

She couldn’t minimize this. Couldn’t frame it as stress or distraction or emotional overload.

She had confronted someone.

She had felt afraid.

And her mind had erased the evidence.

Tears slipped free, hot and silent. She pressed her face into the journal, breathing in the faint scent of paper and ink.

“I’m here,” she whispered. “I’m still here.”

The words felt necessary. Anchoring.

Eventually, the panic ebbed, leaving exhaustion in its wake. Elin lay back against the pillows, staring at the ceiling.

She checked the clock again.

11:03 p.m.

Time was moving now. Normally.

Which meant the damage had already been done.

She opened the journal one last time and wrote beneath the last line.

I need help.

The admission hurt. She’d always been the one who handled things. Who absorbed discomfort quietly? Who made space for other people’s needs?

But this was bigger than her.

This was structural.

She closed the journal and placed it on the nightstand, in plain sight. No more hiding.

If forgetting was the cost of confrontation, then hiding only made it easier.

As she turned off the light, Elin felt the familiar tug at her awareness, the sense of something drifting away.

This time, she didn’t fight it.

She let it go.

Sleep came quickly, heavy and dreamless.

In the morning, she would wake into the aftermath.

And the knowing that this was no longer just happening to her.

It was happening through her.

chapters.title: CHAPTER NINE: Searching for Proof
chapters.content:
CHAPTER NINE: Searching for Proof

Elin woke with the sensation of standing in the aftermath of something large.

Not shock. Not confusion. Aftermath meant the damage had already been done. What remained was the slow work of accounting for what was left.

Morning light filled the room. The journal sat on the nightstand where she’d left it, solid and ordinary. That mattered.

She checked the clock.

7:18 a.m.

Time was behaving.

She sat up and took stock of herself the way she’d learned to do: body first, then mind. No dizziness. No disorientation. The hollow space was there, but it wasn’t widening. Just waiting.

“Okay,” she said softly.

She reached for her phone.

No messages. No calls. No alarms she didn’t remember setting.

She moved through her digital traces quickly, without ceremony. Photos. Call logs. Messages. Nothing past the end of the workday. No record of the evening she knew had happened.

The absence was clean. Thorough.

She opened her calendar.

A block of time waited there, quiet and undeniable.7:00–8:30 p.m.Private.

Created by her.

She stared at it longer than she meant to.

She didn’t remember scheduling it. She didn’t remember attending it. But it existed, asserting itself without explanation.

She took a screenshot and saved it to a new folder.

Evidence.

In the kitchen, she made coffee and narrated the steps under her breath. Water. Grounds. Button pressed. She needed the sequence. The proof of continuity.

The apartment looked lived in. Clean. Ordered. No disruption. No sign of an evening gone wrong.

Which meant it hadn’t gone wrong.

It had simply vanished.

At the table, she opened her laptop and sorted her sent emails by time. Messages from the previous night appeared, measured, professional, unmistakably hers.

She didn’t remember writing them.

A sharp flash of anger cut through her fatigue.

So she could function. Perform. Maintain coherence.

And forget anyway.

She added the emails to the folder and closed the laptop.

If she could do all of this without awareness, then proof was no longer about locating the loss.

It was about measuring it.

She told Calla she was working from home. Calla didn’t argue.

“I’ll check in later,” Calla said.

“Yes,” Elin replied. She meant it.

The morning passed under deliberate observation. Elin set alarms. Left herself notes. Recorded short voice memos explaining what she was about to do, then listened to them afterward to confirm she’d done it.

Everything held.

Which didn’t reassure her.

By early afternoon, structural exhaustion settled in. The fatigue of holding reality together through constant verification.

She called Calla.

“I lost last night,” Elin said when her sister answered.

“All of it?”

“Yes.”

Calla exhaled slowly. “Okay.”

“I found entries I don’t remember writing,” Elin said. “I confronted him again.”

“Again?” Calla asked.

“Yes.”

A pause. “How did you feel afterward?”

Elin swallowed. “I don’t remember feeling anything afterward.”

Silence stretched between them.

“I’m coming over,” Calla said.

“Not yet,” Elin said. “I need to understand this.”

“How fast it’s happening?” Calla asked.

“Yes.”

“You’re not alone,” Calla said.

“I know,” Elin replied. “But I need proof.”

After they hung up, Elin sat very still.

Proof.

The word had changed.

It wasn’t about convincing anyone else anymore.

It was about knowing what was already gone.

As evening approached, she set up a final test.

She placed the journal on the table, open to a blank page. Wrote the time. Wrote how she felt. Wrote what she planned to do next.

Then she set a camera on the shelf, angled toward the room.

She hated the way it felt, turning her life into evidence, but ignorance was worse.

She moved through the evening slowly, aware of the lens. Cooked. Ate. Cleaned. Spoke aloud occasionally, narrating actions like a witness statement.

Nothing slipped.

When she reviewed the recording later, it matched her memory exactly.

Relief washed through her; sharp, almost dizzying.

It’s conditional, she realized.Not constant.

That mattered.

She shut off the lights and sat on the bed with the journal in her lap.

She wrote one final line before sleeping.

Proof exists. But it doesn’t stop the forgetting.

She paused, then added:

It only proves what’s already missing.

The realization settled without drama.

Evidence could confirm the loss.

It could not prevent it.

As exhaustion pulled her under, Elin felt the familiar tug at the edge of her awareness, gentle this time. Almost courteous.

She tightened her grip on the journal.

“Not tonight,” she whispered.

Sleep came anyway.

Whether the night would listen was not up to her.

chapters.title: CHAPTER TEN: The Second Journal Entry
chapters.content:
CHAPTER TEN: The Second Journal Entry

Elin woke with the feeling that she had crossed a line she could not uncross.

She now understood the cost of not preparing. The forgetting didn’t announce itself. It didn’t warn her. It simply acted, efficiently and selectively, leaving her to reconstruct the aftermath.

She sat up slowly and reached for the journal before she reached for her phone.

That, she noted, was new.

The journal opened easily to the last page she’d written, the ink dark and un-smudged. She read the final line again.

Proof exists. But it doesn’t stop the forgetting. It only proves it happened.

She closed her eyes for a moment and let the truth of it settle.

Evidence was not prevention. Documentation was not protection.

But it was something.

She turned to a fresh page and wrote the date and time. She underlined both. Precision mattered now. Context mattered. If she were going to lose pieces of herself, she would leave behind a map.

She titled the page carefully.

SECOND ENTRY; READ FIRST

The words felt heavy, deliberate. A directive, not a thought.

If you are reading this, she wrote, then you have already forgotten something important.

Her pen hovered briefly, then continued.

Do not panic. Panic makes it harder to see patterns.

She paused at that, surprised by the steadiness of the instruction. This version of herself was calm. Strategic. She recognized the voice she used in moments of crisis, when other people needed her to be clear.

She trusted that voice.

She began again, organizing the page into sections.

What You know, Forgetting is tied to emotional confrontation. It accelerates when you challenge it.  It removes context and emotional clarity first. Time loss is possible.

She swallowed and kept going.

What Has Been Confirmed: Other people remember events you do not. You remain functional while forgetting. Written records persist even when memory does not.

She added a line beneath that.

You do not imagine this.

She had a mild panicky feeling as she wrote it, but she did not let herself linger.

What To Do Next: Check the date and time. Read the previous entries. Contact Calla. Do not confront anyone without writing first.

That last instruction gave her pause.

She stared at it, then added:

Confrontation causes loss. Preparation reduces damage.

The language felt clinical, but it was accurate. She had learned that the hard way.

Elin leaned back against the headboard and closed her eyes, feeling the weight of what she’d just done. This was no longer journaling. This was protocol. A system designed to preserve continuity when her mind could not.

She thought of Calla with sharp clarity that surprised her. Her sister’s memory had become a kind of external archive. A living record. That was not a role Calla had asked for, but it was one Elin could not ignore.

She wrote another section.

Anchors: Calla Ellingson (trust her memory) Journal entries (trust the handwriting) Physical environment (photographs, timestamps)

She hesitated, then added a final bullet.

Emotional reactions: (if something feels muted, assume it mattered)

That one hurt.

It meant accepting that numbness was not neutrality. It was loss.

She closed the journal and sat quietly for several minutes, listening to the apartment wake around her. A neighbor’s footsteps overhead. A car door slamming outside. The ordinary world continuing, indifferent to the fact that her relationship with her own memory had fundamentally changed.

Later that morning, she called Calla.

“I’m okay,” Elin said when her sister answered, anticipating the concern. “I mean, stable.”

“That’s not reassuring,” Calla said.

Elin smiled faintly. “It’s accurate.”

They met for coffee near Calla’s office. Elin arrived early and chose a table where she could see the door. Habit, now.

Calla sat down across from her, eyes scanning Elin’s face immediately.

“You look… organized,” Calla said.

“I am,” Elin replied. “Or I’m trying to be.”

She slid the journal across the table.

“I wrote instructions,” Elin said. “For myself.”

Calla hasn’t touched it yet. “Instructions for what?”

“For when I forget again.”

Calla’s jaw tightened. “Elin—”

“I know,” Elin said gently. “But listen. This isn’t spiraling. This is adaptation.”

Calla studied her for a long moment, then opened the journal. She read silently, eyes moving steadily across the page.

When she looked up, her expression had changed to something like reluctant respect.

“You always do this,” Calla said softly. “You turn crisis into structure.”

Elin shrugged. “Structure is safer than hope.”

They sat there, the noise of the café flowing around them.

“What happens next?” Calla asked.

Elin took a breath. “Next, I stop pretending this is temporary.”

Calla nodded once. “And him?”

Elin felt the familiar tug at the edge of her awareness; the emotional outline of something she could no longer fully access.

“I don’t trust my memory of him,” she said carefully. “Which means I trust the fact that I warned myself.”

Calla reached across the table and squeezed her hand. “I’m here,” she said. “Whatever this is.”

Elin nodded, grateful in a way she didn’t try to articulate.

That night, back in her apartment, Elin reviewed her system one more time. Journal accessible. Phone charged. Calendar alerts set. Redundancies layered carefully, deliberately.

She knew it wasn’t foolproof.

But it was intentional.

Before bed, she added one final line to the page.

If forgetting is a response, then awareness is resistance.

She closed the journal and turned off the light.

Sleep came slowly, cautiously, as if testing the boundaries she’d just drawn.

Outside, the wind moved through the trees again, loosening more leaves, carrying them away without ceremony.

Autumn deepened.

And now, Elin was ready for it.

Something is wrong.

I can feel the shape of a memory I can’t reach. Like a word on the tip of my tongue, but heavier. Heavier than it should be.

Everyone else remembers. That’s the worst part. They don’t hesitate. They don’t question. They look at me like I’m supposed to be following along.

I am. I just don’t know how.

chapters.title: CHAPTER ELEVEN: The First Leaf Falls
chapters.content:
CHAPTER ELEVEN: The First Leaf Falls

Elin noticed the leaves before she noticed the memory.

They had gathered overnight along the edge of the sidewalk outside her building, pressed together by wind and rain into a narrow, rust-colored line. Yellow. Brown. A few still clinging to the brittle green they hadn’t fully surrendered yet.

She stopped short, keys still in her hand.

Yesterday, there were fewer.

That was the thing about seasonal change. It didn’t arrive all at once. It accumulated quietly until suddenly it was undeniable.

She stepped carefully over the line of leaves and continued toward her car, the journal’s weight in her bag a familiar reassurance. She had written that morning: time, date, emotional state. Everything was intact. No loss.

And yet.

At work, the air felt different. Not colder, exactly, but thinner. As if the building itself had exhaled something essential overnight.

Elin sat at her desk and opened the journal again, rereading the Second Entry. The instructions felt steady. Useful. She followed them automatically now, checking off steps without needing to think too hard about why.

No new gaps. No immediate danger.

Still, the unease lingered.

Midmorning, Calla stopped by with two coffees.

“You’re hovering,” Calla said, setting one down.

“I’m observing,” Elin replied.

Calla smiled faintly. “Same thing. Different coping mechanism.”

Elin accepted the coffee. “Do you remember when this started last time?”

Calla frowned. “Last time?”

Elin hesitated. “You said I’d been… off before. In past years.”

Calla’s expression shifted; subtle but telling.

“Elin,” she said carefully, “you get quieter in the fall. You always have.”

That wasn’t what Elin had meant. But she nodded anyway.

“Quieter how?” she asked.

Calla shrugged. “More inward. More tired. You pull back.”

“Do I forget things?” Elin asked.

Calla hesitated just long enough to answer the question she hadn’t been asked.

“You repeat yourself more,” she said. “You check things twice.”

Elin’s grip tightened around the coffee cup.

“And do I warn myself?” she asked quietly. “Do I write things down?”

Calla’s gaze sharpened. “Why would you ask that?”

Elin didn’t answer.

That afternoon, she searched her old journals.

Not the current one; the earlier ones she’d stored away, filled with years of half-thoughts and daily fragments. She hadn’t looked at them in months, maybe longer. They lived on the highest shelf of the closet, out of easy reach.

She pulled them down one by one, dust puffing softly into the air.

The first few entries were ordinary. Dates. Weather notes. Small frustrations. The shape of a normal life, recorded imperfectly.

An account of everyday life, documented with inherent limitations.

Then she noticed it.

The handwriting.

Every autumn, it changed.

Not drastically. Not enough to notice at a glance. But the pressure increased. The lines grew tighter. The tone sharpened, became more directive.

And scattered among the entries, she found it.

Warnings.

Not as clear as the current ones. Not as deliberate. But unmistakable.

Remember this.

Don’t trust how calm this feels.

Read this again tomorrow.

Her pulse quickened.

She flipped faster now, scanning years backward.

October. November. Late September.

Each year, the same subtle shift. Each year, the same tone creeping in. Each year, the same inexplicable urgency that disappeared by winter, leaving behind only the written residue.

She sat back on the floor, journals spread around her like fallen leaves.

This wasn’t new.

This was familiar.

The forgetting wasn’t an accident.

It was seasonal.

She wrote it down immediately, hands steady but heart racing.

This happens in autumn.

She underlined it twice.

She tried to recall previous falls; relationships that had cooled inexplicably, decisions she’d deferred without remembering why, emotional distances she’d attributed to stress or burnout.

What if those hadn’t been moods?

What if they’d been aftermath?

The thought settled heavily in her chest.

That evening, she took a walk without a destination, the journal tucked securely under her arm. Leaves crunched beneath her boots. The air smelled of damp earth and smoke.

Everywhere she looked, things were letting go.

She stopped beneath a tree half-stripped of its canopy and looked up. The remaining leaves clung stubbornly to their branches, trembling in the breeze.

How many had already fallen without her noticing?

When she returned home, she checked the journal again. No loss. No gaps. The system was holding.

For now.

She added one more line beneath the day’s entry.

If this is cyclical, then I have survived it before.

The realization brought a strange mix of comfort and dread.

Survival didn’t mean escape.

It meant repetition.

As night settled in, Elin sat on her bed, journal open, listening to the wind scrape leaves along the street below.

The first leaf had fallen days ago.

She just hadn’t known to pay attention.

Now she did.

And the season had only just begun.

chapters.title: CHAPTER TWELVE: Confiding in Someone
chapters.content:
CHAPTER TWELVE: Confiding in Someone

Elin chose the wrong person on purpose.

Not because she wanted to be dismissed, and not because she wanted the reassurance of being believed. She chose the wrong person because she needed a controlled test. If she was going to live with this; whatever it was, she needed to know how it behaved when it left the privacy of her own head.

Calla was too close. Calla already carried pieces of Elin’s continuity for her, and Elin could feel herself leaning into that in a way that scared her. She wanted to prove she could still stand alone. She wanted to see what happened when the story was told to someone who did not automatically become an anchor.

So she chose Mara.

Mara was practical in the way some people were practical as armor. She had a talent for turning messy things into manageable frameworks. Burnout. Stress. Work overload. Anxiety. She believed in the visible world and in explanations that could be acted on. Elin had always liked that about her. It made Mara feel safe.

Safe, Elin realized now, could mean something else too.

Safe could mean sterile.

She almost backed out twice, once while putting on her coat, once while locking the door behind her. Both times, she paused in the hallway, hand still on the knob, and tried to listen to herself. The instinct wasn’t panic. It was resistance. A quiet internal refusal, like the part of her that had started erasing memories, knew exactly what she was about to do.

Tell someone, it seemed to say. And see what it costs you.

Elin went anyway.

They met at a small wine bar just off the main street, a place that softened everything with low light and quiet music. It smelled faintly of citrus and old wood. The air was warm and close, the kind of warmth meant to make people linger.

Elin arrived early and chose a table in the corner with a view of the door. She didn’t like that she did that now. She didn’t like that she thought in terms of exits and angles. Still, she sat down and placed her bag carefully beside her chair, the journal inside it like contraband.
